patient.name: Fatima Begum
patient.complaint: No periods for 8 months, milky nipple discharge and headaches
background: Trying to conceive for a year
Recently clipped a wing mirror while driving

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with hormone excess (galactorrhoea, acromegalic features) and/or mass effect (headache, bitemporal field loss), or a sudden headache in a known adenoma (apoplexy).

points: Fatima, 29, sees her GP: **no periods for 8 months**.
Milky discharge from both nipples; trying for a baby for a year.
Dull **headaches** for 3 months, worse in the mornings.
Recently clipped a wing mirror: 'didn't see the car'.

steps.lead: Fatima's symptoms combine **hormone excess** (milky discharge, no periods) and a **mass effect** (headache, missed car): a pituitary tumour does both.
Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and infertility say **prolactinoma**, the commonest functioning adenoma; the headache and field loss say it is big.

steps.title: Which pituitary tumour?
head: Tumour
Hormone
Key features
rows: Women: amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea; men: ED, gynaecomastia
**Acromegaly**: coarse face, large hands, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea

points: Confrontation fields: she misses targets in both **outer upper** quadrants.
No acromegalic features; no Cushingoid features.
Galactorrhoea on gentle expression; breasts otherwise normal.
Drugs: none. **Not** on antipsychotics or antidepressants.

steps.q: Which visual field defect fits a tumour pressing up on the chiasm?
steps.r: The tumour pushes up from below, catching crossing **inferior nasal** fibres first: both upper temporal fields go first.

steps.lead: Fatima takes no **dopamine-blocking drugs**. A large tumour can also squash the normal gland, causing **hypopituitarism**.
Fatima has no high calcium or ulcers. A prolactinoma with **hyperparathyroidism** or gastrinoma should make you think **MEN 1**.
Fatima is not pregnant and her headache is gradual. A sudden thunderclap headache, vomiting and visual loss would be **pituitary apoplexy**.

steps.text: A **thunderclap headache** with visual loss and ophthalmoplegia is not always subarachnoid haemorrhage: ask about a known pituitary tumour, pregnancy or recent surgery.
Prolactinoma is the most common functioning pituitary tumour: about half of functioning adenomas secrete **prolactin**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'initial' (beta-hCG for hyperprolactinaemia, IGF-1 for acromegaly) versus 'diagnostic' (MRI pituitary, OGTT for acromegaly, insulin tolerance test for hypopituitarism).

steps.q: Fatima has amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. What is the first test?
steps.r: **Pregnancy** is the commonest cause of amenorrhoea and raises prolactin, so exclude it first.

steps.lead: Fatima's **beta-hCG is negative**, her prolactin is very high, and **formal visual fields** confirm chiasmal compression.

steps.title: Pituitary function tests
steps.text: Very high prolactin with low LH (prolactin switches off GnRH); other axes intact.

visual.title: Fatima's prolactin
visual.label: Fatima 6,800
visual.caption: A level this high almost always means a **prolactinoma**. Stalk compression rarely pushes it above a few thousand.

steps.lead: Fatima's **MRI pituitary** shows a 14 mm adenoma lifting the chiasm; full pituitary function tests are already done.

visual.title: Adenoma size on MRI
visual.label: Fatima 14 mm
visual.caption: Over 10 mm is a **macroadenoma**: large enough to reach the optic chiasm.

steps.lead: Fatima's other axes are normal. Suspected acromegaly would need a **glucose tolerance test**; suspected hypopituitarism the **insulin tolerance test**.

steps.text: A random GH level is useless for acromegaly because GH is pulsatile. Screen with **IGF-1** and confirm with an **OGTT**.

management.exam: Expect cabergoline for prolactinoma, transsphenoidal surgery for the rest, steroids first in apoplexy, and cortisol before thyroxine in hypopituitarism.

steps.q: Fatima has a 14 mm prolactinoma compressing her chiasm. First-line treatment?
steps.r: Prolactinomas shrink with **dopamine agonists**, even large ones pressing on the chiasm; surgery is not first-line.

steps.lead: Fatima starts **cabergoline**. An acromegaly or non-functioning tumour would mainly go to **transsphenoidal surgery** instead.

visual.title: Fatima on cabergoline
visual.caption: Prolactin falls within weeks, the tumour shrinks and her fields and periods recover.

steps.title: Treating pituitary tumours
nodes: Any deficiency → replace hormones, cortisol first

steps.lead: Fatima is followed with **prolactin levels and repeat MRI**. If she had hypopituitarism, **cortisol** would be replaced before thyroxine.

steps.text: Giving **levothyroxine before hydrocortisone** in hypopituitarism speeds cortisol use and can precipitate an **adrenal crisis**.

steps.lead: If Fatima's tumour bled (**apoplexy**), she would need **urgent steroids**, neurosurgical review and possibly decompression.
Fatima's care follows **Society for Endocrinology** guidance: test every axis, image, treat by tumour type and monitor.

steps.text: Cabergoline is the answer for a prolactinoma **even with visual field loss**; surgery is reserved for intolerance or resistance.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on why the chiasm gives bitemporal loss, why stalk compression raises prolactin, and why IGF-1 drives acromegaly.

steps.lead: Fatima's tumour is one clone of **lactotrophs**: its effects come from the hormone it makes and the way it grows upwards.
Fatima's adenoma grows up out of the fossa and presses on the **crossing nasal fibres**, so she loses both temporal fields.

steps.title: Why the temporal fields go
nodes: Nasal retina sees the temporal field
Nasal fibres cross at the optic chiasm
Chiasm lies just above the pituitary fossa
Tumour grows up → presses crossing fibres

steps.lead: Fatima's prolactinoma escapes **dopamine** inhibition. A non-secreting tumour pressing the stalk can raise prolactin too: **disconnection**.
In acromegaly, GH drives the liver to make **IGF-1**, which causes the soft tissue overgrowth and insulin resistance.
A bleed into Fatima's adenoma would swell it in the bony **sella**, compressing the chiasm and cutting off ACTH: hence urgent steroids.

steps.text: Prolactin is the only pituitary hormone under **tonic inhibition** (by dopamine), so stalk damage raises prolactin but lowers every other hormone.

mcq.q: What is the most common functioning pituitary tumour?
mcq.r: About half of functioning adenomas secrete prolactin.

mcq.q: Which visual field defect is classic for a pituitary tumour?

mcq.r: Soft tissue swelling compresses the median nerve.

mcq.q: Which is a precipitant of pituitary apoplexy?
MEN 1 combines pituitary tumours with which?
What is the initial test for suspected acromegaly?
mcq.r: IGF-1 screens and monitors; OGTT confirms.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard test for hypopituitarism?

mcq.r: Dopamine agonist; bromocriptine is an alternative.

mcq.q: Which hormone is replaced first in hypopituitarism?
mcq.r: Thyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis.

mcq.q: Why does a non-functioning adenoma raise prolactin?
o: Stalk compression stops dopamine reaching lactotrophs

prompts.q: What are pituitary tumours and how often are they functional?

points.p: Benign monoclonal adenomas of one anterior pituitary cell type
About 75% are functional
Of functional: 50% prolactin, 20% GH, 20% ACTH

prompts.q: What are the mass effects of a pituitary tumour?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: headache plus the field defect.

points.p: Headache, nausea, vomiting
Bitemporal (superior) quadrantanopia from chiasm compression
Hypopituitarism from compression of the normal gland
points.why: Pituitary adenoma is the commonest cause.

prompts.q: How does a prolactinoma present in men and in women?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: men present later with bigger tumours.

points.p: Women: amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, infertility
Men: gynaecomastia, erectile dysfunction, reduced libido and body hair
Drug causes: risperidone, haloperidol, tricyclics, SSRIs

prompts.q: What are the features of acromegaly?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the soft tissue and the risks.

points.p: Coarse facial features, macroglossia
Carpal tunnel, wrist pain, sleep apnoea
Increased colorectal cancer risk

prompts.q: What is pituitary apoplexy and what precipitates it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sudden headache in a known adenoma.

points.p: Sudden retro-orbital headache, vomiting, visual problems
Precipitants: major surgery, coagulopathy, pregnancy
Parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma (95%)
Pituitary prolactinoma or GH tumour (70%)
Pancreatic tumours: insulinoma, gastrinoma (70%)

prompts.q: How do you investigate a suspected pituitary tumour?

points.p: MRI pituitary is gold standard
Full pituitary function: prolactin, GH/IGF-1, ACTH/cortisol, TSH/T4
Formal visual field testing
Hyperprolactinaemia: beta-hCG first

prompts.q: How are acromegaly and hypopituitarism confirmed?

points.p: Acromegaly: IGF-1 first, confirmed by OGTT with failure of GH suppression
Hypopituitarism: insulin tolerance test

prompts.q: How is each pituitary tumour treated, and what is the emergency plan?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: prolactinoma is the medical one.

points.p: Prolactinoma: dopamine agonist (cabergoline, bromocriptine)
Acromegaly: somatostatin analogue (octreotide) and transsphenoidal surgery
Others: transsphenoidal surgery, radiotherapy for residual disease
Apoplexy: urgent steroids, neurosurgical review, decompression
Hypopituitarism: replace cortisol first, then thyroxine, sex hormones, GH
points.why: Thyroxine first can cause adrenal crisis.

prompts.q: Why does a pituitary tumour cause bitemporal hemianopia and raised prolactin?

points.p: Chiasm lies above the fossa; crossing nasal fibres are compressed
points.why: Nasal retina sees the temporal field.

points.p: Prolactin is tonically inhibited by hypothalamic dopamine
Stalk compression blocks dopamine: disconnection hyperprolactinaemia

prompts.q: Why does acromegaly cause tissue changes, and why is apoplexy dangerous?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: IGF-1 and the confined sella.

points.p: GH drives liver IGF-1, which causes soft tissue growth and insulin resistance
Apoplexy swells the gland in the confined sella, compressing chiasm and cavernous sinus
ACTH loss causes acute adrenal insufficiency

glossary.pituitary adenoma: Benign tumour of the anterior pituitary gland.
glossary.prolactinoma: Pituitary adenoma that secretes prolactin; the commonest functioning type.
glossary.prolactin: Pituitary hormone that stimulates milk production and suppresses GnRH.
glossary.acromegaly: Excess growth hormone in adults, causing soft tissue and bone overgrowth.
glossary.GH: Growth hormone, made by somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary.
glossary.IGF-1: Insulin-like growth factor 1, made by the liver in response to GH; the acromegaly screening test.
glossary.Cushing's disease: Cortisol excess from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
glossary.non-functioning: Describes a pituitary tumour that secretes no active hormone.
glossary.galactorrhoea: Milky nipple discharge not related to breastfeeding.
glossary.gynaecomastia: Enlargement of breast tissue in men.
glossary.carpal tunnel: Median nerve compression at the wrist, causing tingling in the fingers.
glossary.sleep apnoea: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, often with loud snoring.
glossary.optic chiasm: Where the optic nerves cross, directly above the pituitary.
glossary.bitemporal hemianopia: Loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes.
glossary.quadrantanopia: Loss of one quarter of the visual field.
glossary.visual field testing: Formal mapping of the visual field (perimetry).
glossary.pituitary apoplexy: Sudden haemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary adenoma; an emergency.
glossary.hypopituitarism: Deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.
glossary.MEN 1: Inherited syndrome of parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
glossary.insulinoma: Pancreatic tumour making insulin, causing hypoglycaemia.
glossary.gastrinoma: Tumour making gastrin, causing severe peptic ulcers.
glossary.beta-hCG: Pregnancy hormone; measured to exclude pregnancy.
glossary.OGTT: Oral glucose tolerance test; GH fails to suppress in acromegaly.
glossary.insulin tolerance test: Insulin-induced hypoglycaemia to test GH and cortisol reserve; gold standard for hypopituitarism.
glossary.pituitary incidentaloma: Pituitary lesion found by chance on a scan done for another reason.
glossary.somatostatin analogue: Drug such as octreotide that inhibits GH release.
glossary.octreotide: Somatostatin analogue used to lower GH in acromegaly.
glossary.dopamine agonist: Drug that mimics dopamine, suppressing prolactin and shrinking prolactinomas.
glossary.cabergoline: Long-acting dopamine agonist; first-line for prolactinoma.
glossary.bromocriptine: Older dopamine agonist used for prolactinoma.
glossary.transsphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
glossary.disconnection hyperprolactinaemia: Raised prolactin because a mass compresses the stalk and blocks dopamine.
glossary.pituitary stalk: Connects the hypothalamus to the pituitary; carries dopamine to the lactotrophs.
glossary.sella: Sella turcica: the bony pocket in the skull base holding the pituitary.
glossary.cavernous sinus: Venous space beside the pituitary containing cranial nerves III, IV, V and VI.
glossary.levothyroxine: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) used as replacement.
glossary.hydrocortisone: Synthetic cortisol, used for replacement and in emergencies.

technique.stem: A 46 year old man has a 1 year history of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction. He has noticed breast swelling and needs to shave less often. He has had headaches for 6 months. He takes no medication. On examination he has gynaecomastia and reduced peripheral vision on both sides.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: hormone symptoms plus a mass effect.

clues: reduced peripheral vision on both sides
steps.x: Hypogonadism with gynaecomastia (hormone excess) plus headache and **bitemporal** field loss (mass).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A pituitary tumour making prolactin: **prolactinoma** (macro, as men present late).

elim: No coarse features, large hands or sweating.
Usually children or young adults, often with DI; less likely here.
Lifelong hypogonadism, no headache or field loss.
Does not explain the headache and bitemporal field loss.

steps.x: **E. Prolactinoma.** Hypogonadism + galactorrhoea/gynaecomastia + bitemporal field loss = prolactinoma.

technique.stem: A 51 year old man has noticed his rings and shoes no longer fit. His wife says he snores loudly and his face has changed. He has numb fingers at night. His BP is 152/94 mmHg. His IGF-1 is raised.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement

steps.x: 'Confirm the diagnosis' means the definitive biochemical test.

clues: rings and shoes no longer fit
steps.x: Enlarging hands and feet, coarse face, sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel, raised IGF-1: **acromegaly**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm with an **OGTT**: GH fails to suppress (or rises paradoxically).

elim: The gold standard for hypopituitarism, not acromegaly.
Would confirm carpal tunnel, not its cause.
GH is pulsatile; a single level is unreliable.
Would confirm sleep apnoea, not acromegaly.

steps.x: **C. Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement.** Acromegaly: IGF-1 screens, OGTT confirms.

technique.stem: A 44 year old woman has acromegaly confirmed by failure of GH suppression on an oral glucose tolerance test. MRI shows an 8 mm pituitary adenoma confined to the sella. Her BP is 148/90 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

steps.x: 'Definitive' asks for the curative option.

clues: 8 mm pituitary adenoma confined to the sella
steps.x: A **microadenoma enclosed** in the sella: surgically curable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transsphenoidal surgery**; somatostatin analogues control GH if surgery fails or is unsuitable.

elim: First-line for prolactinoma; weak effect in acromegaly.
Untreated acromegaly raises cardiovascular and colorectal cancer risk.
For residual or recurrent disease.
A GH receptor antagonist used when other treatments fail.

steps.x: **E. Transsphenoidal surgery.** Enclosed GH adenoma → transsphenoidal surgery; prolactinoma → cabergoline.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has headaches and bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 25 mm pituitary macroadenoma. His prolactin is 1,200 mIU/L (normal less than 400). His tumour shows no hormone staining after surgery.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his raised prolactin?
o: Compression of the pituitary stalk reducing dopamine delivery
Ectopic prolactin secretion by the tumour

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain a mildly raised hormone.
A large **non-functioning** tumour with only a modest prolactin rise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The mass squashes the stalk so **dopamine** cannot reach the lactotrophs: **disconnection hyperprolactinaemia**.

elim: Staining shows the tumour makes no hormone.
No evidence of hypothyroidism.
Not relevant in this man.
No renal disease given.

steps.x: **A. Compression of the pituitary stalk reducing dopamine delivery.** Big tumour + mild prolactin rise = stalk compression, not prolactinoma.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has had no periods for 7 months and a milky discharge from both nipples. Her pregnancy test is negative. She takes no medication. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Very high prolactin causing amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, with pregnancy, drugs and hypothyroidism excluded, is a prolactinoma.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea.
Pregnancy and drugs excluded; very high prolactin with low LH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prolactinoma**.

elim: IGF-1 is normal and there are no acromegalic features.
TSH is normal.
Prolactin this high with galactorrhoea is not PCOS.
LH and FSH would be high, not low.

steps.x: **E. Prolactinoma.** Amenorrhoea + galactorrhoea + high prolactin, not pregnant, no drugs = prolactinoma.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man has increasing hand size, sweating and joint pains. His wife says his jaw and nose have grown and he snores. He has tingling in both hands at night. His BP is 158/96 mmHg and pulse rate 80 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: GH excess drives IGF-1, causing soft tissue overgrowth, prognathism, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea and hypertension.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: soft tissue and bony overgrowth.

clues: tingling in both hands at night
steps.x: Large hands, prognathism, sweating, sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel and hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A GH-secreting pituitary adenoma: **acromegaly**.

elim: Causes central obesity and striae, not bony growth.
Causes coarse skin and carpal tunnel but not jaw growth.
Enlarges the skull but not hands, jaw and soft tissues together.
Hypogonadism and galactorrhoea, not tissue overgrowth.

steps.x: **A. Acromegaly.** Big hands + coarse face + carpal tunnel + sleep apnoea = acromegaly.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma is 1 day after a coronary artery bypass graft. He develops a sudden severe headache behind his eyes, vomiting and double vision. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 86/54 mmHg. GCS is 14.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Major surgery is a precipitant of bleeding into an adenoma; acute ACTH loss explains the hypotension.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: a sudden headache in someone with a pituitary tumour.

clues: sudden severe headache behind his eyes
steps.x: Known adenoma, major surgery (precipitant), retro-orbital headache, ophthalmoplegia and hypotension (ACTH loss).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pituitary apoplexy**: haemorrhage or infarction into the adenoma.

elim: No fever; the known adenoma and surgery point elsewhere.
Does not cause hypotension or ophthalmoplegia.
Would not explain hypotension from cortisol loss.
A key differential, but a known adenoma plus a surgical precipitant favours apoplexy.

steps.x: **C. Pituitary apoplexy.** Known adenoma + sudden retro-orbital headache + vomiting + visual signs = apoplexy.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman has a 2 year history of headaches. MRI shows a pituitary macroadenoma extending upwards from the sella. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?
o: Central scotoma in the left eye
practice.e: Compression of the chiasm from below damages the crossing inferior nasal fibres first, so both upper temporal fields go first.

steps.x: An examination finding question.
Tumour growing **upwards** into the chiasm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Crossing inferior nasal fibres hit first: **bitemporal superior quadrantanopia**, progressing to bitemporal hemianopia.

elim: Optic nerve disease, as in optic neuritis.
Lesion behind the chiasm, such as a right occipital stroke.
Parietal lobe lesion.
Glaucoma or retinitis pigmentosa.

steps.x: **A. Bitemporal superior quadrantanopia.** Pituitary = bitemporal, superior first. Craniopharyngioma (from above) = inferior first.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has 18 months of tiredness, reduced libido and gradually worsening peripheral vision. He takes no medication. MRI shows a 28 mm pituitary mass. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A large tumour with hypopituitarism and only a mild prolactin rise (stalk compression) is non-functioning; a macroprolactinoma gives very high prolactin.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: a large mass with no hormone excess.
Mass effect plus **deficiencies** (low T4 with normal TSH, low testosterone) and only a mild prolactin rise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Non-functioning adenoma** with stalk compression and hypopituitarism; presents late.

elim: IGF-1 is low, not high.
Cortisol is low-normal, not high.
A 28 mm prolactinoma would give a prolactin in the thousands.
TSH would be high; here TSH is inappropriately normal with low T4.

steps.x: **D. Non-functioning pituitary adenoma.** Big mass + low hormones + prolactin only mildly up = non-functioning adenoma.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has a prolactinoma. She has had recurrent kidney stones and a duodenal ulcer that has not healed on omeprazole. Her BP is 130/82 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
practice.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism, a gastrinoma (refractory ulcer) and a prolactinoma together are MEN 1.

steps.x: An underlying cause question: link three tumours.

clues: duodenal ulcer that has not healed
steps.x: Pituitary + **high calcium** (parathyroid) + refractory ulcer (**gastrinoma**).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MEN 1**: parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas.

elim: Medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid; no pituitary.
Neurofibromas and café-au-lait spots.
Can raise calcium but does not cause gastrinoma or prolactinoma.
Haemangioblastomas, renal cancer, phaeochromocytoma.

steps.x: **A. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.** 3 Ps: parathyroid (95%), pituitary (70%), pancreas (70%).

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has had no periods for 4 months and has noticed fluid leaking from her nipples. She takes no medication. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Pregnancy is the commonest cause of amenorrhoea and raises prolactin, so beta-hCG comes first.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation for amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea.
Young woman with secondary amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Exclude **pregnancy** first: **beta-hCG**.

elim: Only after pregnancy is excluded and prolactin is raised.
Confirms acromegaly; not suggested here.
Needed, but pregnancy must be excluded first.
Useful once a mass is found; not first.

steps.x: **C. Serum beta-hCG.** Hyperprolactinaemia work-up starts with a pregnancy test.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has erectile dysfunction and headaches. His prolactin is 5,600 mIU/L. He takes no medication and his TSH is normal. His BP is 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: MRI pituitary is the gold-standard imaging for pituitary tumours, showing size and chiasmal compression.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic investigation' means the gold-standard imaging.
Very high prolactin with headache; drugs and hypothyroidism excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI pituitary** to show the adenoma and its relation to the chiasm.

elim: Less detail of the pituitary than MRI.
Tests for hypopituitarism, not the tumour itself.
For acromegaly.
Obsolete; cannot show the adenoma.

steps.x: **C. MRI pituitary.** Pituitary tumour gold standard = MRI pituitary.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has a 13 mm prolactinoma with a bitemporal field defect. Her prolactin is 7,200 mIU/L. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Dopamine agonists shrink prolactinomas and restore vision; surgery and radiotherapy are second-line.

steps.x: Initial management of a macroprolactinoma.
A prolactinoma, even with chiasmal compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dopamine agonist**: cabergoline shrinks it.

elim: Somatostatin analogue for acromegaly.
Second-line for prolactinoma.
No role in prolactinoma.
Reserved for dopamine agonist intolerance or resistance.

steps.x: **A. Cabergoline.** Prolactinoma = cabergoline first, even with field loss.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman with a known pituitary macroadenoma has a sudden severe headache, vomiting and blurred vision. Her pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg. MRI confirms haemorrhage into the adenoma.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Apoplexy can cause acute adrenal insufficiency, so urgent IV hydrocortisone comes first, then neurosurgical decompression.

steps.x: Initial management of an emergency.
**Pituitary apoplexy** with shock from acute ACTH loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent steroids** (IV hydrocortisone), then neurosurgical review for decompression.

elim: Not for an acute bleed.
Thyroxine before cortisol can precipitate adrenal crisis.
The diagnosis is already made; LP does not treat it.
Not used in apoplexy.

steps.x: **B. IV hydrocortisone.** Apoplexy = steroids first, then neurosurgery.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has hypopituitarism after surgery for a non-functioning pituitary adenoma. His 9am cortisol, free T4 and testosterone are all low. His pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate first hormone replacement?
practice.e: Thyroxine increases cortisol metabolism, so giving it first can trigger adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone goes first.

steps.x: An order-of-replacement question.

clues: cortisol, free T4 and testosterone are all low
steps.x: Several deficient axes, including cortisol.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cortisol first** (hydrocortisone), then thyroxine, sex hormones, GH.

elim: Only if he has DI; not mentioned.
Replaced last, if at all.
Given before cortisol, it can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Replaced after cortisol and thyroxine.

steps.x: **C. Hydrocortisone.** Hypopituitarism: replace cortisol before thyroxine.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has a pituitary macroadenoma growing upwards out of the sella. She has lost the outer half of the visual field in each eye. Her BP is 122/78 mmHg and pulse rate 70 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her visual loss?
o: Compression of crossing nasal retinal fibres at the optic chiasm
Compression of the left optic tract
practice.e: Nasal retinal fibres, which carry temporal field information, cross at the chiasm directly above the pituitary.

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the field defect.

clues: growing upwards out of the sella
outer half of the visual field in each eye
steps.x: **Bitemporal hemianopia** from a tumour pushing up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The chiasm sits above the fossa; **crossing nasal fibres** (which see temporal fields) are compressed.

elim: Causes a right homonymous hemianopia.
Would cause nasal field loss.
Causes homonymous defects.
Glaucoma causes peripheral constriction, not bitemporal loss.

steps.x: **A. Compression of crossing nasal retinal fibres at the optic chiasm.** Bitemporal loss = crossing nasal fibres at the chiasm.
